记录一个可用于定价或反欺诈的数据源。

items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims get the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Read More Breaking Down Silos in Insurance by Rory Meleniclis Insurers can dismantle organizational silos by shifting from project-based work to product teams built around shared capabilities like underwriting and claims. Read More How AI Can Transform Submissions for Underwriting by Prathap Gokul Commercial insurers face a strategic challenge: identifying which submissions merit scarce underwriting attention, not just processing more faster. Read More Making AI Work in Commercial Submission Intake by Vital Soupel Insurers need a practical blueprint for where to apply AI first, how to move beyond pilots, and how to scale the technology responsibly. items.title: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech
items.original_title: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech
items.rss_title: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech
items.rss_description: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech PaulCarroll Mon, 11/16/2026 - 17:10 When I ran the editing operation for the Wall Street Journal's European edition in the '80s, the "lockup" at midnight (or so) was frequently so chaotic that I posited what I called Carroll's law. Building on Murphy's law – everything that can go wrong will go wrong – Carroll's law said Murphy was an optimist. I'm feeling déjà vu , given all the technology-related chaos of the past week, centered on Friday the 13th, when all U.S. air traffic was shut down for hours and Microsoft's Outlook was only intermittently operating after a full-on outage the day before, for what amounts to the email backbone for the world economy. As much as there are individual reasons for those outages and other recent ones, the problems point to a pattern. The transition we're going through to a completely wired, AI world is so fundamental that two things are true: 1) We need to be a lot more careful about work like the upgrades to the FAA system, and we can head off a lot of problems if we are. 2) There will still be chaos from time to time, including for the insurance industry, especially as we start to roll out AI agents. So buckle up. Let's have a look. I first started thinking a couple of weeks ago about writing about the risks that arise from connecting everything to everything through the Internet of Things. The impetus was a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems throughout Europe – including in France, the U.K., Italy, Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg and Estonia – followed by similar attacks on commissaries at U.S. military installations. The hackers raised the temperature inside 900 freezer units across 17 countries to as high as 120 degrees Fahrenheit, causing millions of dollars of food to go bad overnight and be thrown out. France, which suffered two-thirds of the attacks on freezers, blamed Iran, and geopolitical tensions could well lead to such attacks. North Korea, Russia and China all have active military cyber units. It's also possible that teenagers who in the past might have spraypainted graffiti on a school wall will now use AI to indulge their anger and show off in much more destructive ways. In any case, the cyber attacks show that the power of the IoT comes with a potential downside. Connecting essentially every device to every other device gives hackers more routes into systems they want to attack. And industrial systems, such as those that let supermarkets monitor and manage refrigeration centrally typically aren't built to the same security specifications that the main IT systems are. Insurers will have to be alert both about clients and about themselves. Clients may suffer theft, business interruption, claims of negligence against directors and officers, and so on. Insurers may face attacks themselves as they link to more sensors, third-party data sources, and providers of digital services such as payments. Insurers certainly make juicy targets, given all the important information they have on individuals and businesses. The Wall Street Journal published a story with the headline, " Supermarket-Fridge Hacks Show Risk of Linking Everything to the Internet" , that said: "Artificial intelligence suddenly makes the problem much bigger, because hackers are automating their hunt for exposed web connections and running searches at blistering speeds." The article adds that 20% of IoT devices already have at least one known cybersecurity vulnerability. It turns out, though, that the refrigerator cyberattacks were just the start. On Thursday, bleeding into Friday, Microsoft's Outlook email system went down. As Wired wrote in a story headlined " The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World ": " The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge." Full details on the cause of the outage have yet to be provided. At the least, it shows the danger of concentration for a key service such as communication. We've actually seen even more, though smaller, examples of dangerous concentration just since Friday. United Airlines, which controls a major chunk of air travel in the U.S. and internationally, had to delay all departing flights for more than an hour and a half on Monday because of a software issue. A technical glitch with software at Chase Bank delayed online banking and caused transaction glitches for both itself and other major banks. Concentration will only increase from here, so we need to be prepared for the fact that a single problem can cause widespread trouble. There is some speculation that AI may have played a role in the Outlook trouble, given that Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees in July and just offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 people, or 27% of its workforce, while saying the company is turning more coding work over to AI. Which brings us to the FAA communications disaster that shut down air travel for five hours in the U.S. on Friday. The current official explanation is that a single, old router in Arkansas was overwhelmed during an upgrade to new technology, but some officials initially said an upgrade to AI technology known as SMART may also have been involved. Oddly, the disagreement is very public and at the cabinet level – the secretary of Transportation insists the AI work had no bearing on the outage, while the secretary of Homeland Security has suggested at least twice that the AI initiative may have been to blame. Whatever the exact problem, the FAA issue should be the simplest to avoid. It just requires some basic hygiene. For instance, you have to give yourself a way to instantly undo an upgrade if it starts to go south. And whatever you do, you don't do a major upgrade during a busy period -- such as a Friday afternoon, when millions of people are flying somewhere for the weekend. You do the upgrade in the middle of the night, when a problem can be corrected before much of anyone notices. But people will ignore basic principles of software management, just as they'll be too reliant on single sources of key digital services such as communication and will be too slow to tackle the vulnerabilities that come from connecting to systems and services that aren't secure enough. And AI will greatly accelerate the pace at which problems surface. So we should consider recent events as warnings of future problems, not as one-offs. There is good news in the short term, though, for those of you who are superstitious types. Friday wasn't just the 13th; an astrology-curious acquaintance tells me Mercury and Venus both ended their retrogrades that day, bringing some supposed relief after weeks of celestial troublemaking. (Mercury, I'm told, can be especially problematic. It's blamed for everything from miscommunications to travel mishaps.) But both planets have resumed their normal forward movement across the sky, so astrologers give us an all clear – or at least a mostly clear, because the planets' "shadow" periods will last for a few weeks. Cheers,' Paul P.S. I later learned, courtesy of Google, that many people had beaten me to the Carroll adaptation of Murphy's law. Oh, well. P.P.S. My favorite tweet on the tech outages: "If you booked your United Airlines flight through your Chase Bank account and need to access those records on your Outlook, what do you do?" Image Paul Carroll The air traffic debacle and email outage on Friday don't just call for more careful management of our technology. They also offer a stark warning. Building on Murphy's law – everything that can go wrong will go wrong – Carroll's law said Murphy was an optimist. I'm feeling déjà vu , given all the technology-related chaos of the past week, centered on Friday the 13th, when all U.S. air traffic was shut down for hours and Microsoft's Outlook was only intermittently operating after a full-on outage the day before, for what amounts to the email backbone for the world economy. As much as there are individual reasons for those outages and other recent ones, the problems point to a pattern. The transition we're going through to a completely wired, AI world is so fundamental that two things are true: 1) We need to be a lot more careful about work like the upgrades to the FAA system, and we can head off a lot of problems if we are. 2) There will still be chaos from time to time, including for the insurance industry, especially as we start to roll out AI agents. So buckle up. Let's have a look. I first started thinking a couple of weeks ago about writing about the risks that arise from connecting everything to everything through the Internet of Things. The impetus was a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems throughout Europe – including in France, the U.K., Italy, Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg and Estonia – followed by similar attacks on commissaries at U.S. military installations. North Korea, Russia and China all have active military cyber units. Connecting essentially every device to every other device gives hackers more routes into systems they want to attack. Insurers may face attacks themselves as they link to more sensors, third-party data sources, and providers of digital services such as payments. items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?

items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

items.rss_title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_description: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online Life & Health ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:16 Scammers increasingly impersonate insurers to steal identities and money during open enrollment. November 12, 2026 Image Last year, the Justice Department brought the largest healthcare fraud case in its history, which included charges that criminals stole the identities of more than 1 million Americans to submit $10.6 billion in fraudulent Medicare claims for urinary catheters. While Medicare blocked nearly all of it, private Medicare supplemental insurers paid out about $900 million. Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet crime in 2025, up 26% in one year, according to the FBI. Insurance fraud, including healthcare fraud, costs Americans more than $300 billion a year, and health insurance scams pick up during open enrollment, the FTC says. Seniors are the hardest-hit age group, losing $7.7 billion in 2025, up 59% in one year. In fact, Michigan officials warned on Oct. 12 of impostors claiming to be from Medicare to dupe older adults. As co-founder of Spokeo , a people search company, and former co-chair of the W3C Credentials Community Group , I have witnessed firsthand how scammers have grown increasingly sophisticated over the last 20 years. Insurance scams are evolving and costly We are seeing many insurance-related scams in 2026. Fraudsters are buying sponsored search ads with web addresses and logos that look very similar to HealthCare.gov and Medicare.gov . When Americans click on the link, they end up buying a plan that is not real insurance and also fork over their personal information, which can lead to identity theft. Even large health insurers are being duped, as the $900 million loss in the catheter case shows. The Coalition Against Insurance Fraud calls insurance fraud "the crime we all pay for," because it comes back to honest policyholders as higher premiums, which can hurt retention. In a September survey by BrandShield , 30% of U.S. adults said they would stop buying online from brands scammers had impersonated. For an insurer, that is a renewal lost to a scam it never ran. Here are three tips for insurers to help prevent insurance fraud Say what you will never do. Tell customers you will never ask for a one-time code or take payment by gift card, wire or crypto. Put the statement on the ID card, in the app, and on every renewal notice. Explain what numbers to trust and verify. Scammers can spoof caller ID so your company's name appears on a customer's phone. In every fraud alert, encourage customers to use the number on their card and check the identity of incoming callers with a reverse phone search . Report fake ads and websites and warn consumers. Search regularly for impostors using your name and report them to the FBI IC3 , the FTC , and the online platform where they live. Send alerts to customers in real time. Harrison Tang

items.extracted_text: Commercial Property Premium Decreases of 6.2% Drive Overall Soft Q3: CIAB Article 0 Comments Soft market conditions remain stubborn, with no “meaningful” change for average commercial insurance premiums in the third quarter 2026 compared with the prior quarter. The Council of Insurance Agents & Brokers (CIAB)’s latest market survey found premium decreased an average of 1.3% for Q3 across all account sizes. It’s a “slight moderation” of soft conditions from Q2, when premiums decreased an average of 2% across all accounts. “Respondents reported increased competition among carriers for business and increased willingness to compromise on pricing to secure it,” CIAB said in its report. Survey-takers reported decreases in premiums for nine lines of business: business interruption, construction, commercial property, cyber, directors and officers, employment practices, surety bonds, terrorism, and workers compensation. Commercial property recorded the largest decrease in premiums out of all lines at down 6.2% – about the same as Q2. D&O came in next with a decrease of 4.1%, followed by workers compensation, down 3.6%. Decreases grew for D&O, which was down 2.1% the quarter prior. Large account premiums fell by 3.1%, marking a full year of large accounts showed the great decrease of all account sizes, CIAB said. For the 61st straight quarter, commercial auto saw premiums increase, up 6.7% in Q3. Commercial auto premiums increased 4.5% in Q2. Related: Social Inflation Drives Surge in Commercial Auto Liability Claims Outside of commercial auto, all lines of major lines of commercial business – auto, property, workers comp, general liability, and umbrella – showed increases of 3.1% or less. items.extracted_text: Texas Farm Bureau secures $400m Fish Pond Re 2026-1 cat bond at reduced pricing - Artemis.bm Texas Farm Bureau secures $400m Fish Pond Re 2026-1 cat bond at reduced pricing - Artemis.bm Texas Farm Bureau secures $400m Fish Pond Re 2026-1 cat bond at reduced pricing 18th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Texas Farm Bureau Insurance Companies has now successfully priced and finalised its second catastrophe bond sponsorship, securing the 60% upsized $400 million of named storm reinsurance from this Fish Pond Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) issuance at reduced pricing, Artemis has learned. Texas Farm Bureau Insurance, the insurance arm of Texas’s largest non-profit farm organisation, returned to the catastrophe bond market for the second time at the start of the month. This new Fish Pond Re issuance looks set to be a renewal of its soon to mature debut cat bond deal, the $255 million Fish Pond Re 2024-1 whose reinsurance protection draws to a close at the end of 2026. Initially, the Texas Farm Bureau Insurance Companies was seeking $250 million of named storm reinsurance, from this new Series 2026-1 issuance of notes by Fish Pond Re . However, as we then reported in our first update on this offering, the target size for this issuance was increased by 60% to seek $400 million of reinsurance for the sponsor , while at the same time the price guidance was lowered. We’re now told that Texas Farm Bureau Insurance has secured the upsized amount of reinsurance at attractive pricing, which will soon meaningfully increase its capital markets backed reinsurance once this issuance settles next month. As a result, this Series 2026-1 issuance from Fish Pond Re Ltd. will provide the insurer with a $400 million source of fully-collateralized named storm reinsurance protection covering the state of Texas, on an indemnity trigger and per-occurrence basis running through to the end of 2030. The Series 2026-1 Class A tranche of notes were finalised at their doubled $250 million in size. The Class A notes have an initial expected loss of 0.26%. They were first offered with price guidance is in a range from 2.25% to 2.75%, which later fell to between 2% and 2.25% and we’re now told they priced at the bottom-end for a 2% spread to be paid to investors. The riskier Series 2026-1 Class B notes were finalised at their 20% increased $150 million in size. The Class B notes come with an initial expected loss of 0.88%. They were initially offered with price guidance in a range from 3% to 3.5%, which first fell to 2.75% to 3% and now the final pricing was for a spread at the lowest-end again, with 2.75% set to be paid. It’s another very strong result for a catastrophe bond sponsor in 2026, with the market’s price execution and ability to provide meaningful reinsurance limits helping the insurer to boost its capital markets backed protection at attractive pricing. items.extracted_text: RenaissanceRe's third-party capital ILS assets managed rose to $8.63bn in Q3 2026 - Artemis.bm RenaissanceRe's third-party capital ILS assets managed rose to $8.63bn in Q3 2026 - Artemis.bm RenaissanceRe’s third-party capital ILS assets managed rose to $8.63bn in Q3 2026 18th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans RenaissanceRe Capital Partners, the specialist third-party capital management division of the reinsurer, saw external investor capital in its range of joint-venture reinsurance vehicles and insurance-linked securities strategies increase slightly to $8.63 billion through the third-quarter of 2026. The third-quarter was another period of slower growth for the third-party assets under management of RenaissanceRe Capital Partners managed vehicles and ILS funds, as the company both raised and returned capital as it manages available capacity in the current reinsurance market conditions. However, over the last twelve months, RenaissanceRe Capital Partners third-party AUM has still risen by $390 million since January 1st 2026 and stands some $90 million higher than it did twelve months ago. Total partner capital, including RenaissanceRe’s investment stakes in the reinsurance joint-ventures and ILS funds reached almost $10.5 billion as of the end of September, a slight decline over the course of Q3 but still $480 million higher than where this figure sat as of January 1st 2026. RenaissanceRe’s two most significant third-party capital strategies remain the sidecar-like DaVinci Re and the PGGM partnership reinsurer Vermeer Re. DaVinci, which notably celebrated its 25th birthday recently becoming one of the longest-standing third-party reinsurance capital vehicles in the market, stood at $4.99 billion in total capital as of September 30th 2026, with $3.75 billion of that from third-party investors. That is the largest size DaVinci has ever been and it has grown by $550 million since January 1st. Vermeer Re grew in the third-quarter, likely on the back of underwriting and investment profits, to reach $1.94 billion in assets which is again the largest this vehicle has ever been and up from $1.77 billion at January 1st 2026. Fontana, the casualty and specialty lines reinsurance joint-venture has shrunk, which is largely due to a capital return of $100 million through a dividend and also some underwriting losses experienced in the third-quarter , which took the vehicle down to $760 million, of which $510 million is capital from third-party investors as of September 30th. Notably, it appears that thanks to growth of its catastrophe bond strategies and the recent launch of a new cat bond managed account, the $150 million Lighthouse Fund revealed in its Q3 reporting , RenaissanceRe now manages perhaps the most in cat bond related third-party investor AUM in its history at $2.24 billion of the total across Medici, Medici UCITS and the separately managed accounts it also allocates to cat bonds from for investors. Total cat bond assets managed, including RenRe’s stakes in the cat bond funds, reached $2.61 billion by the end of September. As 2026 has progressed, RenaissanceRe Capital Partners have entered a phase of much slower growth, as they look to balance capital with the opportunities available. While at the same time the manager has returned meaningful capital and profits to third-party investors, ensuring they benefit from the recent strong reinsurance underwriting and ILS investment years. items.extracted_text: Root Auto Insurance Is Now Available in Maine Article 0 Comments Technology-driven insurer Root, Inc. is making its personal auto insurance available to drivers in Maine. Using mobile telematics, Root calculates its rates primarily on actual driving performance, such as focused driving, smooth braking, and gentle turns. The system can financially reward safe drivers. Root says safe drivers stand to realize potential annual savings of up to $1,300. Driver onboarding, customized coverage selection, policy management, and claims routing are handled entirely through Root’s mobile app. Root’s personal auto options include liability, collision and comprehensive coverage. Maine becomes the 39th state where Root now offers insurance. The company hopes to offer coverage across the contiguous United States by the end of 2027. It plans to further expand to Massachusetts, North Carolina, Michigan and Idaho pending regulatory approvals. Root also said it plans to expand its independent agent distribution channel to 100,000 eligible producers. Maine agents seeking appointments can apply and be approved in 24 hours. Root also sells through relationships with Carvana, Toyota, and Hyundai Capital. For the third quarter of this year, Root Inc. reported net income of $14.4 million, reversing a loss of $5.4 million over the same period a year ago. For Q3 the combined ratio came in at 97.2 compared with 102.1 a year ago during the same time. In a letter to shareholders, the company’s chief executive officer said competition “intensified” in the personal auto insurance marketplace during the quarter. Alex Timm, co-founder and CEO, said large insurers “increased marketing, broadened underwriting appetite, lowered average premiums, and competed more aggressively for growth.” Root said it completed development of its latest pricing model and began deploying it in the fourth quarter, with the goal of a system that “operates end to end through AI and automation.” At the end of nine months, net income at Root was $75.7 million compared with $35 million in 2025. Root was founded in 2015 and is based in Columbus, Ohio. Topics Auto Maine Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: Citi Settles Sexual Harassment Claims by Managing Director Article 0 Comments Citigroup Inc. settled a high-profile lawsuit by a managing director who claimed the bank had for years tolerated sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination against her. Ardith Lindsey sued Citi three years ago, claiming she’d been the subject of “prolonged, pervasive and outrageous mistreatment” during her 16 years in the bank’s Global Equities Markets division. Lindsey had spent her entire Wall Street career at Citi, starting as the most junior member on the electronic sales trading desk, later taking charge of the desk in 2021, when she was promoted to managing director. A lawyer for Lindsey, Jeremiah Iadevaia, told the court in a letter Friday night that they’d finalized a deal to resolve the case, after months of negotiations. No terms of the agreement were made public. The two sides announced in June that they’d reached a “settlement in principle” after engaging in mediation. Neither Citigroup nor Iadevaia immediately responded to phone messages seeking comment. “Our values and expectations are clear — no one should ever be discriminated against or harassed in the workplace,” Citigroup said in an earlier statement. Lindsey, a University of Virginia graduate, joined Citigroup in October 2007. She alleged that another, more senior, Citigroup executive coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her and her family with violence after she ended it in October 2022. Lindsey’s suit also alleged a sexual assault by a superior when she first started at the bank and claimed there was a “boy’s club” culture at Citigroup’s equities group, including suggestive comments, traders mocking the firm’s sexual harassment policies and frequent outings to strip clubs. The case is Lindsey v. Citigroup Global Markets , 23-cv-10166, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York (Manhattan). items.extracted_text: SafePoint now targeting upsized $125m Nature Coast Re 2026-4 catastrophe bond - Artemis.bm SafePoint now targeting upsized $125m Nature Coast Re 2026-4 catastrophe bond - Artemis.bm SafePoint now targeting upsized $125m Nature Coast Re 2026-4 catastrophe bond 18th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard SafePoint Insurance Company is looking to upsize its fourth catastrophe bond sponsorship so far in 2026, with the target now to secure $125 million of reinsurance protection to add to its recently priced indemnity deal, through this Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-4) issuance, Artemis can report. Earlier this month, SafePoint priced and secured its largest catastrophe bond ever, with the $650 million Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) . That indemnity and per-occurrence cat bond features two tranches of notes, which provides named storm reinsurance protection to the insurer and its reciprocal exchanges. However, as we reported earlier this month, SafePoint returned to the cat bond market to effectively add a third layer that sits above the 2026-2 tranches, so extending the same protection higher up its reinsurance tower. With SafePoint returning to the catastrophe bond market, to further extend on its recently secured cat bond coverage, this clearly demonstrates to any potential cat bond sponsors watching the market closely, that conditions are extremely attractive right now. This latest issuance marks the seventh cat bond offering under the Nature Coast Re Ltd. special purpose insurer, and also marks SafePoint’s twelfth cat bond sponsorship overall. You can read all about SafePoint’s cat bonds in our extensive Artemis Deal Directory . Initially, SafePoint was looking to secure another $100 million layer of reinsurance protection, adding to its Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) issuance, through this new Nature Coast Re Series 2026-4 offering. We’re now told SafePoint is looking to upsize on its cat bond protection, as the targeted issuance size for this new deal has been increased to $125 million. At the same time, we’re told the price guidance has been updated at the mid-point of the initial range. These Nature Coast Re 2026-4 cat bond notes will provide protection to SafePoint Insurance Company itself and the two reciprocal exchanges that the company operates: the Louisiana focused Cajun Underwriters Reciprocal Exchange entity, and the Florida homeowner and business owner focused Manatee Insurance Exchange. The notes will provide fully-collateralized reinsurance protection covering losses from named storms across the states of Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas, which is the same as the Series 2026-2 notes. As we’ve explained before, the coverage tracks the same as well, being on an indemnity and per-occurrence trigger basis. The reinsurance will also run across a four-year period from December 1st, which once again is the same as the Series 2026-2 notes. The now upsized $125 million tranche of Series 2026-4 Class AAA notes have an initial base expected loss of 0.46%. Initially, these notes were first marketed to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 3% and 3.5%. We’re now told that the price guidance range has been revised at 3.25%, so the middle of the initial range. It’s encouraging to see SafePoint continuing to capitalise on market conditions in the cat bond space to lock-in multi-year protection that will give the firm meaningful certainty on its reinsurance for the coming years. Once this latest deal is finalised and priced, this will become SafePoint’s fourth successful catastrophe bond sponsorship this year. The firm first secured $250 million of indemnity protection from the Nature Coast Re 2026-1 cat bond back in February. However, this past month has been exceptionally busy for SafePoint. So far this month, the insurer has secured $750 million of total cat bond protection, as the company recently finalised its largest cat bond yet, as the upsized $650 million Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) deal was priced last week. Then just earlier this week, the company managed to successfully secure its targeted $100 million source of annual aggregate and industry-loss index triggered named storm protection from the Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 issuance. If SafePoint manages to secure its $125 million upsizing for this 2026-4 issuance, it will take total cat bond backed reinsurance limit secured in recent weeks to $875 million for SafePoint and for the year in total to a substantial $1.125 billion. This will make SafePoint one of the biggest cat bond sponsors of 2026 so far in limit terms. As a reminder, you can read all about this new Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-4) catastrophe bond from SafePoint as well as details on almost every cat bond issued in the extensive Artemis Deal Directory . items.extracted_text: IFSCA working group finalises ILS and SPI regulatory recommendations for India - Artemis.bm IFSCA working group finalises ILS and SPI regulatory recommendations for India - Artemis.bm IFSCA working group finalises ILS and SPI regulatory recommendations for India 18th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans A working group convened by India’s International Financial Services Centre Authority (IFSCA) to look at how insurance-linked securities (ILS) could be brought under the country’s insurance regulatory regime has finalised its recommendations, calling for laws to be amended to support a special purpose insurer (SPI) structure. Recall that the subject of a special purpose insurer (SPI) structure for insurance-linked securities (ILS) has been discussed before, with a focus on a potential reinsurance sidecar vehicle. IFSCA’s SPI framework was first unveiled at the 2026 IFSCA-IRDAI Global Reinsurance Summit, earlier this year in Mumbai . IFSCA Chairman K. Rajaraman then said in February that proposals would be sent to the Government of India regarding the regulator’s suggested framework that would allow re/insurers to set up reinsurance sidecars in a special purpose insurance (SPI) structure. The working group recommends the establishment of a regulatory framework, through amendments to the existing insurance code, that would allow for an ILS structure to be used for catastrophe bonds, reinsurance sidecars and other alternative risk transfer use-cases. The group recommends a statutory carve-out under the existing Insurance Act, or another equivalent legislative mechanism be created, to allow for fully-collateralised SPIs to be established and used for cat bonds and other ILS arrangements. Alongside regulatory moves to enable ILS to be transacted in India’s GIFT City under IFSCA regulatory oversight, the working group also calls for the parallel establishment of other expert service providers and capabilities, to enable modelling, actuarial, insurance management and oversight of ILS transactions to be robust and proportionate. The final report of the working group states, “The WG recommends a phased implementation strategy comprising legislative enablement, notification of a dedicated regulatory framework, ecosystem development. The first step would involve obtaining targeted statutory carve-out under the Insurance Act, 1938 or such other legislative mechanism as may be considered appropriate. This would be followed by the formulation of comprehensive regulations governing SPIs and ILS within GIFT IFSC. “The WG believes that GIFT IFSC is uniquely positioned to emerge as a regional hub for catastrophe risk financing. As a unified financial regulator overseeing insurance, banking, capital markets and fund management within an international financial centre, IFSCA possesses institutional advantages that enable the seamless regulation of ILS across their entire lifecycle. By combining internationally aligned regulation with a supportive market ecosystem, GIFT IFSC can attract global catastrophe risk capital, enhance India’s financial resilience against natural disasters.” They expect the development of ILS regulations and the supporting ILS market infrastructure will be phased, with catastrophe bonds seen as an initial and principal product, around which market capacity and capabilities develop. “Once the foundational ecosystem has matured, the scope may progressively be expanded to other forms of insurance-linked and alternative risk-transfer structures, including reinsurance sidecars, collateralised reinsurance and other sophisticated ART vehicles. This approach would allow market participants and regulators to build experience progressively while establishing the specialised service providers, modelling capabilities, legal expertise, transaction-management infrastructure and investor base required for a deeper ILS market,” the working group stated. The final report provides “a roadmap for establishing an internationally credible ILS framework in GIFT IFSC,” the working group explains. Adding, “The proposed approach is firmly grounded in comparative international practice, consistent with the supervisory principles of the IAIS and supported by a clear legal and prudential rationale for distinguishing fully collateralised SPIs from conventional insurance companies. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. As we’ve explained before, this is another industry-loss triggered catastrophe bond being issued through reinsurance broker Gallagher Re’s operated Arthur Re Ltd. platform that helps make issuance of industry-loss index trigger cat bonds more cost effective and efficient. The ceding entity to this Arthur Re Ltd. – Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond is Lloyd’s syndicate 2001, while the coverage is also set to benefit sub-syndicate 1673, both of which are managed by MS Amlin Underwriting Limited and underwrite for the MS Amlin arm of the global Mitsui Sumitomo insurance group. Initially MS Amlin linked Syndicate 2001 and sub-syndicate 1673 were looking to secure a $100 million source of multi-peril and multi-regional retrocessional reinsurance protection from this cat bond deal. Now we’ve been told, that the syndicate’s are looking to upsize their protection, as the targeted issuance size for this deal has increased by 50% to $150 million. At the same time, the price guidance for the notes on offer has been updated to a tighter spread within the upper-half of initial guidance. So, Arthur Re Ltd. is now offering and looking to sell a $150 million tranche of Class A notes to investors on behalf of a segregated account named Kanata Re 2026-1. These Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond notes are designed to provide Syndicate 2001 and sub-entities with a multi-year source of fully-collateralized multi-peril and multi-regional retrocessional reinsurance from the capital markets. These notes will provide Syndicate 2001 and sub-entities with protection on an annual aggregate and industry loss index trigger basis. Covered perils and regions include U.S. named storm, U.S. and Canada earthquake, and European windstorm events. The protection is designed to run across a four-year term, comprising four calendar year annual aggregate risk periods, beginning from the start of 2027 and ending in 2030. The now upsized $150 million tranche of Class A Kanata Re 2026-1 notes come with an initial attachment probability of 3.01% and an initial expected loss of 2.524%. Initially, these notes were first marketed to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 4.5% to 5%. Sources have now told us that the price guidance range has narrowed to between 4.75% and 5%, so the upper-half of the initial range. It appears that the MS Amlin syndicates are looking to capitalise on investor appetite in the cat bond market to lock in even more multi-peril and multi-regional retrocessional protection than they originally sought. While they may have benefitted from cat bond protection in the past through the group, this Kanata Re 2026-1 sponsorship marks the first time they are the named ceding entities. It’s also important to highlight that Gallagher Re’s Arthur Re platform continues to be increasingly utilised by cat bond sponsors to gain access to the capital markets for index-triggered reinsurance protection. items.title: Florida Stormwater Ponds Become Floating Solar Farms as Costs Fall, Demand Rises
items.original_title: Florida Stormwater Ponds Become Floating Solar Farms as Costs Fall, Demand Rises
items.rss_title: Florida Stormwater Ponds Become Floating Solar Farms as Costs Fall, Demand Rises

items.extracted_text: Florida Stormwater Ponds Become Floating Solar Farms as Costs Fall, Demand Rises Article 0 Comments Of the tens of thousands of retention ponds designed to collect runoff during Florida’s frequent downpours, some are also being used to generate solar power, expanding sustainable energy production in the Sunshine State. Floating photovoltaics — solar panels mounted on buoyant structures anchored in reservoirs and ponds — have become less expensive since the technology emerged two decades ago. They can generate electricity without competing for scarce available land, and the cooling effect of the water may even boost output. Researchers caution, though, that the cost of water-based solar remains high and the environmental impact is not fully understood. After about 20 years, “people have started to believe, have started to see that it works, that it’s fairly reliable, and that lenders and investors have also gained confidence in the technology,” said Oktoviano Gandhi, a scientist at the Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute. While the United States has been slow to adopt the technology, Florida’s geography, climate and development history make it particularly well suited for floating solar projects to address growing electricity demand. Sustainability Goals Fuel Solar Expansion The median reported cost of floating solar projects fell from $2.41 per watt in 2015 to $1.25 per watt in 2024, a decline of about 48%, Gandhi said. Nevertheless, floating solar still costs more upfront than comparable land-based solar. He said published comparisons suggest a premium of roughly 10% to 25%. While adoption of the technology has grown since the first pilot was installed in Japan in 2007, Gandhi said, floating solar accounts for less than 1% of global solar capacity. By the end of 2024, more than 9.6 gigawatts of floating solar generating capacity had been installed in 66 countries and regions , Gandhi said. Rafael Almeida, a freshwater ecosystem scientist and assistant professor at Indiana University Bloomington, said floating solar’s growth is part of the broader expansion of solar energy development, driven by demand for renewable and lower-carbon electricity. “It’s not like only floating solar is increasing,” Almeida said. “All kinds of solar energy, ground-mounted, in particular, has been accelerating over the past decade.” About 90% of global floating solar power-generating capacity is in Asia and about half of that is in mainland China, Gandhi said. The technology is well established in China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, where land is at a premium, while the United States is lagging mainly because it has more land available for energy development, Almeida said. His research group found about 95% of floating solar sites are on managed waters, including reservoirs in Japan, quarry lakes in Europe and aquaculture systems in China. In the U.S., utilities, municipalities and other public agencies may already control bodies of water in places with high power demands. Floating solar systems have been installed on water treatment ponds and sewer facilities across the country, and even on a winery irrigation pond in Napa Valley, Gandhi said. Florida explicitly supports floating solar through a state law that was enacted in 2022 . Justin Kramer, director of emerging technologies and data analytics at the Orlando Utilities Commission, said available land is limited and expensive. “Floating solar provides locations that are within the city limits, but they’re not being used for anything else,” Kramer said. The state’s towns and cities have an estimated 76,000 stormwater ponds , amounting to about 2.7% of its urban land area, according to University of Florida researchers, based on 2012 land-use data. AJ Reisinger, an associate professor at the university who specializes in urban soil and water quality, said Florida has so many stormwater ponds because of its heavy rainfall, flat terrain, sandy soil and development history. Experts said the suitability of a body of water depends on proximity to the electrical grid, water levels, anchoring conditions, size, competing uses, economics and environmental considerations. The commission started out with a 32-kilowatt system that it expanded and then developed a separate 120-kilowatt project. In November 2025, it launched the 2-megawatt Conway Road array , a floating system comprising more than 3,400 panels that the Orlando commission says is the state’s largest floating solar installation. D3Energy says it holds exclusive rights to develop floating solar systems on eligible Florida Department of Transportation stormwater ponds within state highway rights-of-way, and estimates those systems could generate more than 1 gigawatt of energy. Florida Operators Say Systems Have Weathered Hurricanes The floating systems produce about 5% to 8% more power than a typical rooftop array because of the cooling effect of the water, Kramer said. Gandhi cautioned this benefit is sometimes overstated and varies considerably, depending on wind and ambient temperatures. The panels can reduce evaporation, which Gandhi said is especially useful on irrigation reservoirs in dry regions. Kramer said Orlando’s arrays are designed for changing pond levels and Florida wind speeds, and have operated through multiple hurricanes. They are “designed to go up and down as the stormwater pond levels increase or decrease,” he said. “And they’re designed for the wind speeds that we have to deal with.” D3Energy, which has more than 15 floating solar projects in Florida, said none of its systems suffered structural damage when Hurricane Milton slammed the Gulf Coast in 2024. Stormwater ponds are engineered infrastructure, but they also support algae, plants, bacteria, insects, fish and birds. They can also help manage nutrients, pollutants and sediments. “They definitely do conduct and perform a lot of the same natural ecological processes and ecosystem functions that we would expect from a natural pond or a natural wetland,” said Reisinger at the University of Florida. Floating solar can also limit the amount of sunlight entering the water. Reisinger said shading can alter photosynthesis and primary production, potentially changing algae, submerged plants, nutrient removal, habitat and aquatic food webs. While covering part of a water surface can cool the water and reduce evaporation, it can also change the amount of oxygen available to the aquatic ecosystem, Almeida said. The Orlando commission tries to limit the coverage to 70% to 80% of a pond’s surface the exact amount depends on maintenance needs and the pond’s ecosystem, Kramer said. Scientists do not yet know how much coverage is too much. “Are there tipping points after which you start changing the system in ways that the nature of the system is dramatically changed?” Almeida said. “At what levels should we stop covering?” Top photo: An array of solar panels floats atop a pond at Nova Southeastern University, in Davie, Florida. items.extracted_text: Japan to Launch Natural Disaster Warning Network Across Asia Article 0 Comments Japan will create a network across the Asia-Pacific region to promote development of early-warning systems aimed at bolstering protections against extreme weather events and natural disasters. Gaps in capabilities such as remote sensing and cellphone alerts have been highlighted by recent events, including the devastating August floods near the Nepal-China border, which killed more than 1,400 people and wiped out towns, border posts and hydropower plants “The network will share knowledge and expertise in the introduction and operation of the early warning systems and promote effective deployment,” Japan’s Environment Minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa said Tuesday in a speech to the COP31 conference in Antalya, Turkey. Japan, which lies on an arc of volcanoes and fault lines surrounding the Pacific Basin known as the “Ring of Fire,” has been a pioneer in earthquake early-warning systems and developing buildings designed to withstand powerful tremors. The country also remains committed to supporting countries with climate finance, though sees a need for other nations to contribute more, Sasagawa said. “To meet the needs of countries requiring support, it is essential to broaden the contributor base to include countries capable of contributing, and to expand various financial flows including private finance,” he said at the conference. Developed economies have persistently called for the likes of China, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states to expand their climate finance contributions, while those nations argue that most responsibility should rest with countries that industrialized first. items.extracted_text: Texas Medical Marijuana Legalization Gains Momentum But Hurdles Remain Article 0 Comments Sarah Todd, director of the Texas Cannabis Policy Center, felt confident that James Talarico would win his U.S. Senate seat on election night, but when she witnessed a complete blue wave wash over the state, she felt something else: optimism for an adult-use cannabis market in the Lone Star State. “I’m very surprised and now very excited for this new day in Texas,” Todd said. “I think we have a very clear path to adult legalization in Texas.” Lawmakers last week filed a slew of proposals ahead of the legislative session that starts in January, including several that would legalize, tax and regulate marijuana in Texas. Adult-use cannabis bills have been submitted by lawmakers for the past several legislative sessions, but Republican-dominated health committees and the Senate often squashed them before they got far. Todd said this is due to soon-to-be former Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who made it a priority to ban THC products last legislative session. But with new THC-friendly leadership being established in multiple state positions, the concept of legalizing marijuana has never been closer to a reality, Todd said. “There are Republican senators who believe in cannabis law reform, and it remains to be seen what the environment in the Senate is going to be,” she said. “But I’m very hopeful and positive that we’re going to be having a lot different conversations than we’ve ever had in the past.” If an adult-use cannabis program is approved in Texas, it will join a growing list of states that have created entire industries off a plant, but what that might mean for the current THC market in the state still needs to be figured out. “Part of what we are working on is making sure that all stakeholders have a voice in this process,” Todd said. The THC market in Texas The legal THC market in Texas is almost entirely hemp-derived products sold by licensed retailers. The only legal marijuana available to the public is the Texas Compassionate Use Program, which is meant for patients who meet specific medical conditions. Hemp and marijuana are pretty much the same thing, coming from the same plant, with the real distinction between the two being how much THC it contains when harvested. Under the 2018 federal farm bill, hemp with no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC became legal nationwide, leading to a booming industry in Texas with farmers, distributors and stores quickly taking advantage of the rule change to sell legal high-inducing products to the public. The Texas Department of State Health Services lists about 14,000 retail stores licensed to sell consumable hemp, with the industry generating around $300 million a year in state tax revenue. Over the past year, state rules and court rulings have narrowed the hemp market sharply, and a looming federal ban coming next month is putting more pressure on the shrinking legal THC market in Texas. DSHS earlier this year passed new rules on the hemp industry enforcing a 0.3% total THC limit that eliminates smokable hemp, which makes up more than half of some stores’ inventory. A federal funding deal will also ban hemp-derived products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC, criminalizing nearly all consumable hemp nationwide and effectively shutting down the $8 billion industry in Texas. Lukas Gilkey, chief executive of Hometown Hero, a manufacturer of hemp-derived products, said industry leaders plan to speak with lawmakers to discuss market protections and clarity on their future. “We’re going to start working with lawmakers to repeal all of this nonsense immediately,” he said about the state rules. However, some drug policy experts say that, due to the growing number of restrictions, it might be easier to bring an adult-use cannabis market forward to avoid clashing with the federal government over hemp. “Texas could also consider creating a more comprehensive legal cannabis market, as 24 other states have done, and allow smokable cannabis through that channel,” Katharine Neill Harris, a drug policy fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, previously said. Todd said part of her organization’s goal is to ensure hemp distributors, farmers and store owners are brought into the fold of the adult-use cannabis market or allowed to work in tandem with it. “None of these early-filed bills had any language to indicate how lawmakers were thinking about handling the existing hemp THC market,” Todd said. “We had some meetings with the lawmakers that filed the bills to make sure that’s on their radar to ensure this is handled in a thoughtful way to allow these small-business owners who employ over 50,000 people in Texas to continue to operate.” In the past, medical cannabis license holders have often clashed with the hemp industry due to what they viewed as unfair state regulations being placed on them when a similar plant was being sold unchecked. However, the medical cannabis program has seen some of these restrictions slowly rolled back, and Nico Richardson, CEO of Texas Original, said the midterm election results create an opportunity to expand the Texas Compassionate Use Program and improve patient access even further. “We are grateful for the support of leaders on both sides of the aisle who have helped more Texans access the medicine they need,” he said. “As we approach the 2027 legislative session, strong safety standards for all THC products and expanded access to well-regulated medical cannabis should remain priorities.” Jervonne Singletary, a spokesperson for the Austin medical marijuana company goodblend, said her company has always believed that Texans deserve safe, reliable access to cannabis, whether as a patient or as an adult, but some questions need to be answered first. “Who will test these products and make sure consumers can trust what is on the label? What standards will apply to how cannabis is grown and manufactured? What products should be available? What rules make sense around packaging and advertising? And just as importantly, how do we make sure patients continue to have a medical program that works for them?” she said in an emailed statement. Singletary said the medical cannabis community welcomes the conversation around adult-use cannabis, but legalization is only part of the conversation. “Texas also has to make sure the right infrastructure is in place to support it,” she said. “At the end of the day, people access cannabis for a myriad of reasons, and we should respect those choices. There is room for a strong medical program and a responsible adult-use market to exist side by side.” Todd agreed, saying she believes medical cannabis, adult-use marijuana and hemp-derived products can all coexist because each person might want different items or products despite it coming essentially from the same plant. “I know in Minnesota they have put in place some regulations that allow their adult-use retailers and license holders to continue selling cannabis, and then you get lower-potency hemp-derived products over the counter and then a separate higher-strength medical cannabis program,” she said. How would legal cannabis work? Two bills filed by Reps. Joe Moody, D-El Paso, and John Bucy, D-Austin, both titled the Texas Regulation of Cannabis Act, would let adults 21 and older possess 2 ounces of cannabis, including up to 15 grams of concentrate. The bills would also allow adults to grow up to 12 plants at home, and local governments couldn’t ban or unreasonably restrict marijuana businesses. The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation would oversee the market. Retail sales would carry a 20% tax on top of sales tax, and grower-to-retailer sales a separate 15% tax. Tax revenues would fund public schools, veterans assistance programs, chemical dependency prevention, treatment and rehab services and local governments for regulation and oversight. A bill filed by Sen. Carol Alvarado, D-Houston, similarly set rules, regulations and protections for cannabis users and distributors. Todd said while these bills are a great start, there are many things that still need to be discussed before adult-use cannabis is ready to be established in Texas, even if it does receive approval from lawmakers and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa. “First and foremost, I think it’s imperative to pass some decriminalization along with legalizing for adults,” she said. “Decriminalization of low-level possession has been a priority of ours for a long time.” Several years ago, five Texas cities voted to decriminalize having small amounts of marijuana, but Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton sued them to block their ordinances from going into effect. Todd said that with Paxton being replaced by Democrat Nathan Johnson, who has supported decriminalization in the past, next year is a prime opportunity to take this effort statewide and safely establish the adult-use cannabis market. “Decriminalization passed the House last session, and we really had good traction before it died in the Senate, like it does every time. I believe that we can really get it passed this time around and it will happen in tandem with an adult-use bill,” she said. Todd said one benefit of the hemp markets’ rise in Texas over the past several years is that it creates a blueprint for lawmakers to use to create an adult-use marijuana industry. She said hemp-derived products prove the demand is there now it’s important to ensure a legal marijuana market is done correctly. “We don’t want this to look like other states,” Todd said, who has previously criticized the bills Moody and Bucy proposed as too much of a tax burden on retailers and growers. “I think every other state that’s gone before us has made some pretty serious mistakes that have really hampered retail, specifically with overtaxation and overregulation.” Even if lawmakers approve legal cannabis, it may take a couple of years to establish in Texas because the state must go through the rulemaking process, distribute licenses, and build facilities. Todd said that while there is still a long way to go before an adult-use marijuana market is established in Texas, she is feeling positive and hopeful about the future for the first time. “I think that we have a real chance of getting the plant to the people,” she said. “We have a really big opportunity here in Texas to do it a little bit differently and to do it really sensibly.” Disclosure: Rice University has been a financial supporter of The Texas Tribune within the past five years. items.extracted_text: Waymo Halts Freeway Rides After Crackdown by California DMV Article 0 Comments Alphabet Inc.’s Waymo robotaxi unit temporarily suspended freeway driving after California regulators imposed fresh restrictions on the company, the latest setback for the leading self-driving vehicle operator in the U.S. California’s Department of Motor Vehicles barred Waymo from testing or operating on all freeways in the state after finding the company’s driverless operation on those roads posed “an imminent hazard to public safety,” the department said in a statement. The DMV cited multiple instances incidents involving Waymo’s vehicles, including one in which three robotaxis entered an active construction zone on a closed stretch of U.S. Route 101 south of San Francisco. Waymo in turn restricted freeway operations across its other markets to evaluate its performance, the company said in a statement. No collisions or injuries were involved in the California incidents, Waymo said, and its robotaxis continue to operate on surface streets. The company said it’s working with the DMV and other state officials to resume freeway operations. Waymo is facing growing scrutiny by state and federal authorities over episodes in which its vehicles fail to obey basic rules of the road that human drivers encounter routinely. Although Waymo is by far the biggest U.S. robotaxi operator with the most autonomous miles driven, the issues show how the technology continues struggle with some real-world scenarios. Waymos failing to yield for school buses in Austin have drawn the attention of local officials and federal auto safety regulators. The company in June recalled thousands of robotaxis for a software fix to prevent them from entering construction zones, with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration citing 13 such cases in Phoenix and San Francisco in April and May alone.
